doc.title: Jerry Bergonzi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 7, 2022

title: Two-year waiting list and offers from Berklee and New England Conservatory
summary: After leaving Brubeck in 1981 he took private students, built a two-year waiting list, and was then offered positions at Berklee and NEC.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Did you have to do some serious — well let me rephrase. I’m going to guess that maybe you started teaching a few private lessons and then to move to a university level did you have to codify some of your own methods and prove to some committee that you were worthy of being there?

Actually no I didn’t. I had already codified a lot of — because I had, when I moved back to Boston after leaving Dave Brubeck in 1981, the end of ’81, I put up little flyers and in a short amount of time I had a two year waiting list. Two years. And if you want to study with me okay you can but you’re on a list, two years. And it really was a two year waiting list. And so after years of doing that and having all the teachers from Berklee

study with me — and not all of them but most of them you know, and they’re teaching my stuff and I didn’t even think about it. This is what I teach. And the only reason I was good at it was because I taught myself. Nobody showed me so I had to learn how to play. And it’s the only thing I wanted to do is be a better player. So I would get systems for myself to practice. But then Berklee called me up and offered me a position for low bread. And I said I don’t even have to leave my apartment, I’ve got a two year waiting list, I don’t have to pay for parking and I’m getting paid more. I’m good. New England Conservatory called me up and said, “Jerry what do you want?” I said this. They said, “Okay, no problem.” So and that’s not a put down for Berklee. At the time that’s just where they were at you know.
